newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU, U.S. narrow gap on product recognition talks.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. narrow gap on product recognition talks.

text.p: Talks between the European Union and the United States on easing trade in pharmaceutical and other products failed to produce an agreement on Tuesday, but officials on both sides said the gap between them had narrowed.

On the sidelines of the OECD meeting, EU trade commissioner Sir Leon Brittan put proposals to U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky, aimed at getting an agreement whereby the European Union and the United States recognise each others product inspection procedures.
The agreement would allow products approved in EU states to enter the United States without further checks and vice-versa.
A stand-off between the camps over pharmaceutical and medical devices remains. Agreement over telecommunications and electrical equipment has been largely worked out.
U.S. officials estimate that the overall products covered by such an agreement would be worth $40 billion, according to an EU official.

"We have made a lot of progress, but there are one or two points outstanding," an EU official told reporters as the EU delegation prepared to leave the OECD Paris headquarters where they had been negotiating.
"There is a moderate to high chance of reaching an agreement tomorrow," the official said.

Sources said the U.S. Federal Drugs Administration, which has proved reluctant to give up its powers to accept or reject European products, had been moving its position during the talks. U.S. officials said last week, when the talks stalled in Washington, that the FDA was concerned consumer safety would be threatened.
"We have narrowed our differences," a U.S. official told reporters. "We expect an agreement eventually, but not today."

Earlier, EU officials said that they had set themselves the deadline of agreement by the time U.S. President Bill Clinton met European Comission President Jacques Santer, which takes place on Wednesday.
